before: Every medicine sold lawfully in a regulated market carries a control the buyer never sees. Before a licensed drug reaches a patient, its manufacturer must show that the trace metals left behind by synthesis, catalyst residues, reagent contamination, leachables from equipment, sit below a permitted daily exposure derived from toxicology. That control is the International Council for Harmonisation's Q3D guideline, adopted in the United States Pharmacopeia as General Chapters <232> and <233>, and it sets an explicit daily limit for two dozen elements, route by route: one ceiling for a drug you swallow, a tighter one for a drug you inject, a tighter one still for a drug you inhale [2][3].
after: ICH Q3D describes risk-based elemental-impurity controls for drug products within its scope, using permitted daily exposures for oral, parenteral, and inhalation routes. USP General Chapters <232> and <233> address impurity limits and analytical procedures. These frameworks have defined scopes and do not universally require testing every lot; HMTc’s proposed testing controls are separate program decisions [2][3].

before: Peptides, SARMs, and research chemicals never meet that control, because they are never licensed drugs. The Food and Drug Administration treats selective androgen receptor modulators as unapproved drugs and has warned both companies and the public against selling and using them in body-building products [4]. It treats the gray-market and counterfeit versions of injectable peptide hormones, the semaglutide and tirzepatide analogs sold outside the approved supply chain, as unapproved and, in the counterfeit case, as a direct danger, seizing product and warning consumers not to use it [5]. Anabolic-androgenic steroids sold for muscle growth are controlled substances and unapproved drugs at once. None of these products passes through a new-drug application, so none is ever assessed for elemental impurities under Q3D. They are also, by the same legal status, not dietary supplements and not foods, so the contaminant limits that govern those categories do not reach them either.
after: FDA identifies SARMs marketed for bodybuilding as unapproved drugs and warns consumers against their use [4]. Its warnings also address products advertised for research while being sold for human use. Lack of approval is a quality-assurance problem, not a legal exemption. FDA’s separate notices describe counterfeit Ozempic and nonsterile compounded semaglutide and tirzepatide; counterfeiting and compounding are distinct issues, and lawful compounding operates under specific conditions [5].

before: The result is a class defined by absence. There is no lawful product heavy-metal content limit for a gray-market peptide anywhere in the world, and no certification framework has previously addressed it. The framework built to keep metal out of an injection, the one that would matter most here, because injection is the dominant route, applies only to the licensed products these are sold as alternatives to. The absence is not a technicality. It is the reason the buyer of an unregulated injectable has no assurance that a regulated patient is given as a matter of course.
after: HMTc has not identified a category-specific government concentration limit to adopt for this grouping of gray-market products. That program finding does not establish that the products are exempt from drug law, that no quality requirements apply, or that testing makes them lawful. The question addressed here is whether the metal content has been measured reliably.

Brands should maintain one controlled state-law register per SKU family, not one national baby-food checklist. The register should cite the official statute, show current status and date, record the operative product definition, list metals and method requirements, identify the disclosure URL or QR destination, and name the owner who rechecks the rule. It should point to the certification record rather than copying test results into unmanaged spreadsheets. The register also needs a negative statement: what the rule does not do. Virginia does not become federal law; Vermont's product definition does not automatically apply in Illinois; and FDA's planned cadmium or inorganic-arsenic work is not binding until the agency issues an instrument with legal effect. That negative control prevents a fast-moving state landscape from becoming an internally inconsistent set of claims. The Heavy Metal Index’s Closer to Zero overview provides background on selected federal action levels; it is a secondary reference, not the state-law register itself 6.
